blocks.text: A loss function is a specific kind of objective function, the one used throughout machine learning to measure exactly how wrong a model prediction is compared to the true answer. Where the previous lesson covered objective functions in their most general form, spanning maximization goals like reward alongside minimization goals like cost, this lesson narrows the focus to the machine learning specific case, a number that is almost always meant to be pushed down toward zero.

blocks.caption: A loss function turns a prediction and a true value into one error score

1. Loss Function as a Special Case of Objective Function

Every loss function is an objective function, but not every objective function is a loss function. A loss function specifically compares a model prediction against a known true value and outputs a single number representing the size of the mistake. Because it measures a mistake, a loss function is defined so that lower is always better, unlike a general objective function which might just as easily be framed as something to maximize.

This narrower definition is precisely why the word loss almost never appears attached to a reward signal in reinforcement learning or an accuracy score in a report, those are objective functions describing something desirable being maximized, while loss specifically describes an undesirable error being minimized.

blocks.title: A quick vocabulary check
blocks.content: Objective function is the umbrella term from the previous lesson. Loss function is the specific, error measuring member of that family used almost everywhere in supervised machine learning training loops.

blocks.text: 2. The General Shape of a Loss Function

A loss function takes two inputs, the value a model actually predicted and the true value that was supposed to be predicted, and produces one output, a nonnegative number describing the size of the mistake. When the prediction matches the true value exactly, a well designed loss function returns zero, and the value grows larger the further the prediction drifts from the truth.

code.content:
def loss(prediction, true_value):
    # a placeholder shape every real loss function follows
    error = measure_of_difference(prediction, true_value)
    return error   # 0 when perfect, larger for bigger mistakes

blocks.text: Across an entire training set, the loss is usually computed per example and then averaged, giving a single number that summarizes how the model is doing across every example seen so far, not just one.

blocks.text: 3. Why Loss Functions Are Almost Always Minimized

A loss function measures wrongness, and there is no version of wrongness that anyone wants more of. This is why, unlike the general objective function from the previous lesson which could be framed either way, loss is essentially always something to push toward zero. Training a model is the search for parameter values, weights, that make this single loss number as small as possible across the training data.

items: Loss near zero means predictions are close to the true values.
Large loss means predictions are far from the true values.
Training success is judged by whether loss reliably decreases over time.

blocks.text: 4. Mean Squared Error and the Mean

Mean squared error, MSE, computes the average of the squared difference between each prediction and its true value. Squaring the difference makes every error positive and makes larger errors count disproportionately more, a prediction that is off by 10 contributes 100 times more to the loss than a prediction that is off by 1.

blocks.title: Why MSE is tied to the mean
blocks.content: The value that minimizes the average squared distance to a set of numbers is exactly their mean, the topic covered in the statistics module. This is not a coincidence, MSE is built directly on the same squared distance idea that defines the mean, which is why a model trained to minimize MSE effectively learns to predict something like a conditional mean of the target given the input.

blocks.text: 5. Mean Absolute Error and the Median

Mean absolute error, MAE, computes the average of the plain, unsquared absolute difference between each prediction and its true value. Every unit of error counts the same amount toward the total, a prediction off by 10 contributes exactly 10 times more than a prediction off by 1, not 100 times more as with MSE.

blocks.title: Why MAE is tied to the median
blocks.content: The value that minimizes the average absolute distance to a set of numbers is exactly their median, also covered in the statistics module. A model trained to minimize MAE is therefore effectively learning to predict something like a conditional median, which is far less sensitive to extreme outlier values than the mean is.

blocks.text: 6. Comparing MSE and MAE

Because MSE squares every error, it punishes large mistakes heavily and pushes a model hard to avoid them, which is useful when big errors are truly much worse than small ones. Because MAE treats every unit of error equally, it is far more robust to a handful of extreme outliers in the data, since one wildly wrong prediction cannot dominate the total loss the way it would under MSE.

blocks.text: 6.1 A Blended Option: Huber Loss

Huber loss behaves like MSE for small errors and like MAE for large errors, switching between the two at a chosen threshold. This gives much of the smoothness of MSE while limiting how much a single extreme outlier can dominate training, a practical middle ground used in several production regression systems.
7. Cross Entropy Loss for Classification

MSE and MAE both compare two numbers directly, which works naturally for regression tasks that predict a continuous quantity. Classification tasks instead predict a probability distribution over classes, and the standard loss function there is cross entropy, covered in full detail in the information theory module cross entropy lesson, which measures how far a predicted probability distribution sits from the true one.

The short version worth repeating here, cross entropy penalizes a confident wrong prediction far more heavily than a mildly wrong one, which pushes a classifier to become genuinely well calibrated rather than merely correct on average. Anyone who has not yet read the cross entropy lesson in the information theory module should treat that lesson as the natural next stop after this one for the classification side of loss functions.
7.1 Categorical Cross Entropy for Multiple Classes

When there are more than two classes, categorical cross entropy generalizes the binary form, comparing a full predicted probability vector against a one hot true label vector across every class at once. It reduces to plain binary cross entropy exactly when there are only two classes to choose between.
8. Choosing a Loss Function for the Task

The loss function must match the shape of the prediction task. Regression tasks predicting a continuous number typically use MSE, MAE, or Huber loss. Classification tasks predicting a category typically use cross entropy in its binary or multiclass form. Ranking tasks, object detection, and other specialized problems often use their own tailored loss functions built from these same underlying ideas.

blocks.title: Matching the loss to the real cost of a mistake
blocks.content: A medical screening model and a product recommendation model can both be framed as binary classification, yet the real world cost of a false negative versus a false positive is wildly different between them, a good loss function design should reflect that asymmetry rather than treating every mistake as equally costly by default.

blocks.text: 9. How the Choice of Loss Function Shapes What a Model Learns

A model never sees the real world goal directly, it only ever sees the loss function score computed from its predictions. Whatever the loss function rewards with a lower score is exactly what the model will drift toward during training, echoing the same lesson from the objective function chapter, an optimizer faithfully pursues precisely what it is told to minimize.

Swapping MSE for MAE on the same dataset can noticeably change the fitted model, since MSE trained models bend toward avoiding a few very large errors while MAE trained models are comparatively indifferent to a handful of outliers, treating them the same as any other mistake of similar absolute size.

blocks.title: A concrete illustration
blocks.content: Given housing price data with a few extremely expensive mansions mixed in with ordinary homes, an MSE trained model will distort its predictions for ordinary homes somewhat in order to reduce the enormous squared error on the mansions, while an MAE trained model will largely ignore the mansions as a small number of equally weighted outliers.

items: MSE trained models lean toward predicting something close to a conditional mean, sensitive to outliers.
MAE trained models lean toward predicting something close to a conditional median, robust to outliers.
Cross entropy trained classifiers lean toward well calibrated probabilities, not just correct top guesses.

blocks.text: 10. Loss Function Versus Evaluation Metric

The loss function used during training is not always the same as the metric reported to describe final performance. A classifier is commonly trained against cross entropy, since it is smooth and differentiable, but reported afterward using accuracy or F1 score, since those are easier for a human to interpret even though they cannot be used directly to guide gradient based training.

This split exists because a good training signal and a good reporting number often have different requirements, a training loss needs to be differentiable and to provide useful gradient information at every point, while a reporting metric needs mainly to be interpretable and aligned with business goals.
11. Regularization Terms Added to a Loss Function

In practice, the loss function minimized during training is often the raw prediction error loss plus an extra penalty term, called a regularization term, that discourages overly large model weights. This combined loss still fits the exact same shape as a plain loss function, one number to minimize, it simply bundles in an additional preference for simpler models alongside the preference for accurate ones.

code.content:
def regularized_loss(y_true, y_pred, weights, alpha=0.01):
    data_loss = mse(y_true, y_pred)
    penalty = alpha * np.sum(weights ** 2)   # L2 regularization term
    return data_loss + penalty

blocks.text: This penalty term is exactly why a regularized model sometimes accepts a slightly higher raw prediction error in exchange for meaningfully simpler, more generalizable weights, the combined loss is still what gets minimized, and simplicity is now genuinely part of what counts as a good score.
12. Loss Functions in Code Frameworks

Deep learning frameworks ship a standard library of ready to use loss functions, so practitioners rarely need to implement MSE or cross entropy from scratch in production code. Selecting the right one from the library, rather than writing a custom one, is usually the correct first move for a standard regression or classification task.

code.content:
import torch.nn as nn

mse_loss = nn.MSELoss()
mae_loss = nn.L1Loss()
bce_loss = nn.BCELoss()
ce_loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

blocks.text: Reaching for a custom, handwritten loss function is usually reserved for genuinely nonstandard tasks, ranking, structured prediction, or a business specific tradeoff between error types, where none of the standard library options faithfully capture what good actually means for that particular problem.
13. Worked Example: Computing MSE and MAE by Hand

A small regression model predicts house prices, in lakhs, for three houses. The true prices are 50, 65, 40, and the model predicted 55, 60, 45. Compute both MSE and MAE for these three predictions by hand.

code.content:
true_prices = [50, 65, 40]
predicted = [55, 60, 45]
print(mae(true_prices, predicted))   # (5 + 5 + 5) / 3 = 5
print(mse(true_prices, predicted))   # (25 + 25 + 25) / 3 = 25

blocks.text: In this particular example every error happens to be exactly 5, so MAE comes out to 5 while MSE comes out to 25, illustrating directly how squaring inflates the reported loss value even when the underlying mistakes are identical in absolute size.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Using MSE on data with extreme outliers and being surprised the fitted model bends heavily toward them.
Feeding raw, unnormalized logits into a loss function that expects already normalized probabilities, or the reverse.
Treating the loss value as directly comparable across two different datasets or two different loss functions, when the numeric scale is not the same.
Forgetting that a lower training loss does not automatically mean better real world performance, especially once overfitting sets in.
Picking a loss function by habit rather than by matching it to the actual shape of the prediction task and the cost of different kinds of mistakes.

blocks.text: A related trap worth calling out on its own, comparing MSE from one experiment against MAE from another as if they measure the same thing, they are on entirely different numeric scales and are not a fair basis for choosing between two models.

Another easy slip, evaluating a classification model purely on training loss while ignoring a held out validation set, a steadily falling training loss alongside a rising validation loss is the classic signature of overfitting, not genuine improvement.
15. Practice: Compute Loss for a Small Dataset

A weather model predicts tomorrow temperature, in celsius, for four days. True temperatures are 20, 22, 19, 35, and predicted temperatures are 21, 22, 20, 25. Notice the fourth day has a much larger error than the rest, a genuine outlier.

code.content:
true_temps = [20, 22, 19, 35]
predicted_temps = [21, 22, 20, 25]

# TODO: compute mae(true_temps, predicted_temps)
# TODO: compute mse(true_temps, predicted_temps)
# Compare how much the single outlier on day 4 changes each result

blocks.text: Expect MSE to be pulled up dramatically by the single large error on day four, while MAE rises by a smaller, more proportionate amount, a direct hands on demonstration of the outlier sensitivity difference covered earlier in this lesson.

As a follow up exercise, try replacing day four's true temperature with 26 instead of 35, removing the outlier entirely, and recompute both losses, MSE should drop far more sharply than MAE, since it was the squared outlier term dominating the total in the first place.

blocks.title: Looking ahead in this module
blocks.content: The next lesson steps back to look at the overall shape of loss functions and objective functions as landscapes, convex functions with one single bowl shaped minimum versus non convex functions with several dips and bumps, which directly determines what kind of optimization guarantee gradient descent can offer.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

A loss function is the machine learning specific objective function that measures how wrong a prediction is against a known true value, and it is almost always meant to be minimized. MSE ties back to the mean and punishes large errors heavily, MAE ties back to the median and treats every error proportionately, and cross entropy, covered fully in the information theory module, handles the classification case by comparing probability distributions.

The choice of loss function is not a minor implementation detail, it directly determines what a trained model ends up optimizing toward, which is precisely why the next lessons in this module, covering gradient descent and its variants, matter so much, they are the machinery that actually searches for the parameters minimizing whichever loss function has been chosen here.

The pattern from the previous lesson repeats here in a more specific form, defining the loss function precisely, MSE, MAE, or cross entropy, is a design decision made before training even starts, and the search algorithm that follows can only ever be as good as the number it is handed to optimize.
